citation: Lynn SK et al. Validity and reliability of surface electromyography measurements from a wearable athlete performance system. J Sports Sci Med 2018;17:205-215
status: published; no correction found in search
exercise_muscle_contraction: VL, VM, BF on isokinetic dynamometer
hardware_processing: Athos textile EMG garment vs research-grade sEMG, concurrent
results_effects_uncertainty: No significant system effect on repetition amplitude (95th pct, peak, sum); normalised rep-amplitude variability 10.7% (research) vs 12% (Athos). Agreement statistics (LoA) not seen
limitations_coi: n=12; isokinetic lab conditions not free weights; non-significance read as equivalence risk; funding/COI not verified (could not open full text)
tentsr_applicability: Shows a wearable garment can match lab amplitude in a controlled task; says nothing about spectral fatigue, dry studs, or free-weight gym use

citation: Colyer SL, McGuigan PM. Textile electrodes embedded in clothing: a practical alternative to traditional surface electromyography when assessing muscle excitation during functional movements. J Sports Sci Med 2018;17(1):101-109
exercise_muscle_contraction: running, cycling, squatting; VL, BF, glute max
hardware_processing: textile EMG shorts vs gel surface electrodes, separate sessions
results_effects_uncertainty: Agreement acceptable at low amplitude, poorer at high amplitude; textile bursts systematically longer; between-session CV of ARV ~41-43% for both systems
limitations_coi: not concurrent; small n; males only; manufacturer of shorts not confirmed from snippet
tentsr_applicability: Between-day amplitude CV ~40% even with gel electrodes argues against absolute between-day amplitude features; burst duration depends on electrode type/threshold

citation: Saucier DN et al. External load and muscle activation monitoring of NCAA Division I basketball team using smart compression shorts. Sensors 2021
results_effects_uncertainty: Muscle-load variables differed by position for some groups; authors note little research on sEMG effectiveness for coaching metrics
limitations_coi: no criterion reference; discriminating positions is not validity
tentsr_applicability: Illustrates that a commercial 'muscle load' metric is published with no criterion validation

citation: Gonzalez-Badillo JJ, Yanez-Garcia JM, Mora-Custodio R, Rodriguez-Rosell D. Velocity loss as a variable for monitoring resistance exercise. Int J Sports Med 2017;38(3):217-225
results_effects_uncertainty: Equations predicting % reps completed from velocity loss; described as fairly precise; high absolute reliability (values not seen)
tentsr_applicability: Comparator baseline for any TENSR RIR claim: bar-velocity methods exist and must be beaten or matched

citation: Garcia-Ramos A et al. (barbell velocity vs repetitions in reserve). Int J Sports Physiol Perform 2018
results_effects_uncertainty: Generalised group equations gave unacceptable between-subject variability; individualised relationships needed
tentsr_applicability: Implies any TENSR RIR model will likely need per-user calibration

citation: Zhao H, Kurokawa T, Tajima M, Liu Z, Okada J. Understanding perceived exertion in power-aimed resistance training: the relationship between perceived exertion and muscle fatigue
hardware_processing: sEMG RMS and MDF (hardware not seen)
results_effects_uncertainty: RPE, velocity loss and MDF differed across volume (p<0.001); RMS did not; no significant MDF-velocity loss relationship
limitations_coi: p-values only seen; effect sizes not seen; small n
tentsr_applicability: MDF and velocity loss are not interchangeable fatigue markers; amplitude did not track volume

citation: Yan et al. Study on the differences in peripheral fatigue responses elicitation effects of bench press training with different loads and tempos based on electromyography and motion sensors. Front Physiol 2025
exercise_muscle_contraction: bench press 60/80% 1RM, fast vs 2/0/2/0 tempo; pec major, ant delt, triceps
results_effects_uncertainty: Significant load x tempo interaction for all fatigue markers incl. MDF decline; largest MDF drop at 80% fast
tentsr_applicability: Directly contradicts the brief's 'MDF fatigue is tempo-independent' as a general statement

citation: Authors UNVERIFIED. Changes in EMG and movement velocity during a set to failure against different loads in the bench press exercise. Scand J Med Sci Sports 2021
exercise_muscle_contraction: bench press to failure at 40/60/80% 1RM, max intended velocity; pec major, triceps
results_effects_uncertainty: sEMG amplitude higher mid/late set vs initial at all loads; MDF drop larger at lighter loads
tentsr_applicability: MDF decline magnitude at failure depends on load, so a single MDF threshold for 'failure' is not expected to transfer across loads

citation: Ruiz-Alias et al. Validity and reliability of velocity and power measures provided by the Vitruve linear position transducer. PLoS One 2024
exercise_muscle_contraction: back squat free weight and Smith
results_effects_uncertainty: Acceptable reliability; validity criteria not met for most variables (fixed/proportional bias); only Smith peak velocity acceptable
tentsr_applicability: Even dedicated bar-velocity devices show bias vs criterion; sets the evidence bar a velocity claim must meet

citation: Weakley J et al. The validity and reliability of commercially available resistance training monitoring devices: a systematic review. Sports Med 2021
results_effects_uncertainty: Most studies lacked gold-standard criterion; LPTs more accurate than other device types (secondary summary); accelerometers questionable
tentsr_applicability: IMU-on-limb velocity estimates should be expected to be weaker than bar-mounted LPTs

tentsr_applicability: Hint that simple IMU timing features may carry much of the signal; TENSR must test EMG added value over IMU baseline
